sweep_summary: Ten titles swept for viet1252 (catalog: no-word-stress, deciding source Brunelle 2017 JIPA, quotation re-verified in the held text). Four new open texts fetched sources and read into ( and updated with URLs and md5s): Michaud 2005 Paris 3 thesis (HAL; tone/intonation, silent on word stress; only a phrase-boundary remark that demarcative marking falls on the last lexical syllable before extrametrical final particles), Jannedy 2007 ISIS 8 (Potsdam; focus prosody, silent, repeats Thompson's pause-group stress), Ha 2012 A-PL monograph (ANU; intonation of short utterances, silent), and Schiering, Bickel & Hildebrandt 2010 JL (CORE mirror of the ZORA postprint; the published form of the Glottolog 'Does Vietnamese have prosodic words?' talk), which explicitly denies a separate word-stress layer and places stress at the phonological-phrase level — confirms the coding, does not supersede Brunelle 2017. Not obtainable: Henderson 1966 (archive.org lending only; Firthian syllable analysis, low priority), Ingram & Nguyen 2007 MKS 37 (sealang refused connections; medium priority as the main competing experimental work), Nguyen, Ingram & Pensalfini 2008 (paywalled; abstract only, L2 English), Ha 2013 De Gruyter chapter (paywalled; conversation prosody), Lanh 1980 Russian avtoreferat (not found; sentence intonation). Nothing found contradicts the catalog; no recode suggested.org, ANU DSpace, Potsdam OPUS and UQ eSpace APIs directly.

new_statements.quote: The acoustic evidence from the production experiments does not support the idea of a separate layer of word stress in Vietnamese. (p.671) ... To summarize, Vietnamese provides ample evidence for a genuine stress domain that is preferably disyllabic and maximally trisyllabic. Within this domain, stress is realized on the final syllable in the default case. Crucially, this domain is computed irrespective of the morphosyntactic status of its constituent syllables, i.e. stress phonology does not distinguish between a word-level and a phrasal-level of prosodic structure. Metrically, polysyllabic words are thus indistinguishable from other combinations of syllables. (p.672)
new_statements.citation: Schiering, René, Balthasar Bickel & Kristine A. Hildebrandt. 2010. The prosodic word is not universal, but emergent. Journal of Linguistics 46(3): 657-709. doi:10.1017/S0022226710000216
new_statements.reading: Vietnamese has no word-level stress: prominence is assigned within a phrase-level stress unit (2-3 syllables, final syllable strong by default, semantic salience overriding), identically for words and phrases; polysyllabic words are metrically indistinguishable from phrases. This is a typological synthesis of Thompson 1965 and the Ingram & Nguyen experiments, not a new instrumental study, and it agrees with the catalog's no-word-stress coding.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (54 pp, ZORA postprint of the CUP typeset version, running footers carry the published page numbers 657-709;..) and. Both quoted passages are verbatim, but the page locators are off by one: '2.2.2 Stress and the polysyllabic word' begins on p.670 (txt line 707, footer 670 at line 742); 'The acoustic evidence from the production experiments does not support the idea of a separate layer of word stress in Vietnamese.' is on p.672 (txt lines 819-820; extracted text of PDF page 17 shows the sentence at layout line 28 with footer 672), not p.671; 'To summarize, Vietnamese provides ample evidence for a genuine stress domain... Metrically, polysyllabic words are thus indistingu…
new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: No correction to the bearing. Refinement only: Schiering et al. deny a WORD-level stress layer but still posit a genuine phrasal stress domain (iambic, final by default, semantic salience overriding, Sino-Vietnamese compounds left-branch), assigning stress to the Phonological Phrase (p.673); Brunelle 2017 goes further and denies stress altogether, reinterpreting final prominence as phrase-final lengthening. Both are consistent with the catalog's NO-WORD-STRESS / domain WORD coding.

sources.citation: Phạm, Andrea Hoà. 2008. Is there a prosodic word in Vietnamese? Toronto Working Papers in Linguistics 29. 23 pp.
sources.quote: Reviews the views (Emeneau: equal energy on every syllable; Thompson: three degrees, phrasal; Cao 1978: stress by syntactic relation) and asserts, citing her own unpublished ms., that 'Vietnamese appears to be an iambic language, i.e., each foot consists of a weak syllable followed by a strong one (Pham, ms)'; the paper's own evidence is clitic reduction (tone survives, segments delete), argued to show a prosodic word exists; explicitly does 'not attempt to account for stress patterns'. Impressionistic, no measurements; this is one of the iambic claims Brunelle 2017 tested and rejected.
sources.locator: §2.2 'Stress in Vietnamese: how significant is it?', pp.4-5 (txt 158-225)

sources.citation: Nguyen, Thu & John Ingram. 2006. Acoustic and perceptual cues for compound-phrasal contrasts in Vietnamese. Speech Prosody 2006, Dresden. doi:10.21437/speechprosody.2006-178
sources.quote: 'there was no significant effect on any of the acoustic parameters between compounds and noun phrases elicited under the picture naming task ... Even under conditions of maximal contrast, there is no significant acoustic evidence to support the claim about the contrastive stress patterns between compounds and noun phrases in Vietnamese.' Differences found are juncture / word-final lengthening of the first constituent of phrases (45 speakers, Hanoi, Hue, Saigon).

sources.citation: Jannedy, Stefanie. 2007. Prosodic focus in Vietnamese. Interdisciplinary Studies on Information Structure (ISIS) 8: 209-230.
sources.quote: Thus, it appears that local changes in the f0 as we know them from stress accent languages such as English and German, appear to play a role in the expression of focus in Vietnamese. We are reluctant at this point to call these local prominences 'accents' as this term has a specific meaning in the literature. Rather, we term them accentual prominences that are clearly visible for the subject and verb focus conditions. (p.224)
sources.note: Pilot production/perception study of focus marking (Hanoi speakers): focus is expressed prosodically (f0, duration, amplitude trade-off) with no focus particles. On lexical stress it only reproduces Thompson (1965:106) — heavy/medium/weak stress distributed over the pause group by information load — and offers no statement of word-stress placement. Silent on the coding.

sources.citation: Michaud, Alexis. 2005. Prosodie de langues à tons (naxi et vietnamien), prosodie de l'anglais: éclairages croisés. Thèse de doctorat, Université Paris 3 - Sorbonne Nouvelle. 538 pp.
sources.quote: en vietnamien, elles [les particules finales] portent un ton lexical au même titre que les autres syllabes, mais le marquage des frontières (accent démarcatif de la terminologie évoquée en section 3.1.1) a lieu sur la dernière syllabe lexicale qui précède les particules finales (...) ; les particules sont donc « extramétriques », et peuvent être dites « inaccentuées », tout en précisant que cette absence d'accent ne commande pas de neutralisation tonale. (pp.210-211) [Translation: in Vietnamese the final particles carry a lexical tone like any other syllable, but boundary marking (the 'demarcative accent' of §3.1.1) falls on the last lexical syllable preceding the final particles ...; the particles are thus 'extrametrical' and may be called 'unaccented', with the proviso that this absence of accent entails no tonal neutralisation.]
sources.locator: Ch. III (Hanoi Vietnamese tone/intonation experiment, pp.143-166); Ch. IV §3.1.6 'Entre système tonal et système accentuel', pp.208-211 (txt lines 9432-9570)
sources.note: An instrumental study of intonational emphasis on Hanoi Vietnamese tones (126 monosyllables, three tones, F0 and open quotient), compared with Naxi and English. Vietnamese is classed throughout as a 'langue à tons modulés complexes' opposed to English as 'langue à accent'; its lexical tones are what the thesis counts as its 'accentuation'. The only word-level prominence statement is the phrase-boundary remark quoted (boundary marking on the last lexical syllable before extrametrical final particles), plus a general discussion of weak syllables in tone languages. No claim about stress placemen…
